title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
Vim and its modern extension Neovim are highly efficient, terminal-based modal text editors. Unlike standard text editors, Vim segregates typing text from executing navigation commands by utilizing different “modes.”
In this tutorial, we will cover the core modes, key navigation, essential commands, and how to resolve one of the most common friction points for new users: setting up seamless copy-pasting to and from the system clipboard.

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
1. The Core Concept: Modal Editing
When you open Vim or Neovim, you start in Normal Mode. You cannot type text immediately; instead, keys on your keyboard act as shortcuts for moving around and editing the file.
There are three primary modes: * Normal Mode (Default): For navigation, deleting, copying, and pasting text. Press Esc to return to this mode from any other mode. * Insert Mode: For writing text. Enter this mode by pressing i (insert before cursor) or a (append after cursor). * Visual Mode: For selecting blocks of text. Enter this mode by pressing v (character-wise) or V (line-wise).

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
2. Essential Navigation & Commands
All of these commands are executed from Normal Mode.

Navigation (HJKL)
Avoid the arrow keys. Use these keys to keep your fingers on the home row: * h: Move left * j: Move down * k: Move up * l: Move right


Basic Editing Commands

x: Delete character under cursor.
dd: Delete (cut) the entire current line.
yy: Copy (yank) the entire current line.
p: Paste (put) copied text after the cursor.
u: Undo the last action (Ctrl + r to redo).



Command Line Mode (Ex Commands)
Press : to enter command line mode, then type: * :w: Save changes (write). * :q: Quit Vim. * :wq: Save changes and quit (equivalent to :x or ZZ). * :q!: Quit without saving changes.

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
section: 3. Configuring Copy-Paste to the System Clipboard
text:
3. Configuring Copy-Paste to the System Clipboard
By default, when you copy (yank) text using y or delete text using d, Vim stores it in its internal registers, not your system’s global clipboard. This means you cannot paste yanked text into your web browser or another application.
To bridge this gap, Vim uses special registers: * + represents the system clipboard (global copy/paste). * * represents the primary selection (middle-click paste).

Step 1: Verification
First, verify that your Vim or Neovim installation has clipboard support compiled in.
For Vim, run:
vim --version | grep clipboard
If you see +clipboard or +xterm_clipboard, clipboard integration is supported. If you see -clipboard, you need to install a version of Vim with GUI support (like vim-gtk3 on Ubuntu or gvim on Arch).
For Neovim, clipboard support is handled through external utilities. You must install the appropriate tool for your display server:
# For X11 (Arch Linux / Ubuntu)
sudo pacman -S xclip xsel     # Arch
sudo apt install xclip xsel    # Ubuntu

# For Wayland (Arch Linux / Ubuntu)
sudo pacman -S wl-clipboard   # Arch
sudo apt install wl-clipboard  # Ubuntu


Step 2: Configuring Auto-Clipboard Integration
Rather than typing special keys to access the clipboard registers every time, you can configure Vim/Neovim to automatically route all yanks and deletes directly to the system clipboard.

For Vim:
Edit your ~/.vimrc:
nano ~/.vimrc
Add the following line:
" Automatically sync Vim registers with the system clipboard
set clipboard=unnamedplus


For Neovim:
Edit your configuration file: * If using Lua (~/.config/nvim/init.lua): lua   -- Sync Neovim register with system clipboard   vim.opt.clipboard = "unnamedplus" * If using Vimscript (~/.config/nvim/init.vim): vim   set clipboard=unnamedplus



Step 3: Copying & Pasting Manually (Without configuration)
If you are on a server and don’t want to change your global configuration, you can target the system clipboard register (+) explicitly:

To Copy (Yank) to Clipboard:

Highlight text in Visual Mode (v).
Type: "+y (Double quote, plus sign, yank).

To Paste from Clipboard:

In Normal Mode, place the cursor where you want the text.
Type: "+p (Double quote, plus sign, paste).

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
If you spend a lot of time in the terminal, you have likely run into the limit of managing multiple terminals, tabs, and windows. This problem is amplified when connecting to remote servers via SSH; if your network connection drops, your running processes die.
Tmux (Terminal Multiplexer) solves these problems. It allows you to run multiple terminal sessions inside a single window, split your screen into panes, and detach sessions so they run in the background even if you log out.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
1. Core Concepts of Tmux
Tmux organizes your workflow into three hierarchical structures: 1. Sessions: A session contains one or more windows. A session runs in the background and stays alive until the server restarts or you explicitly kill it. 2. Windows: Similar to tabs in a web browser, a window occupies the entire display screen. 3. Panes: You can split any window into multiple rectangular areas called panes, each running its own shell.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
section: 2. Managing Sessions from the Command Line
text:
2. Managing Sessions from the Command Line
Before launching tmux, you manage sessions using the standard system terminal.
# Start a new session with a random name
tmux

# Start a new session with a descriptive name (Recommended)
tmux new -s dev

# List all active tmux sessions
tmux ls

# Attach to the last active session
tmux a

# Attach to a specific named session
tmux attach -t dev

# Kill/Delete a specific session
tmux kill-session -t dev

# Kill all active tmux sessions
tmux kill-server

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
3. Session Navigation: The Prefix Key
Once inside a Tmux session, all keyboard commands must be preceded by the Prefix key. By default, the prefix key is:
\[\text{Prefix} = \text{Ctrl} + \text{b}\]
To execute a command, press Ctrl + b, release both keys, and then immediately press the command key.

Essential Keyboard Shortcuts

Session Operations

Prefix + d: Detach from the current session (leaves it running in the background).
Prefix + $: Rename the current session.
Prefix + s: List and switch between active sessions.



Window (Tab) Operations

Prefix + c: Create a new window.
Prefix + ,: Rename the current window.
Prefix + n / p: Move to the Next or Previous window.
Prefix + 0 through 9: Select window by index number.
Prefix + &: Kill (close) the current window.



Pane Operations

Prefix + %: Split the window vertically (left and right panes).
Prefix + ": Split the window horizontally (top and bottom panes).
Prefix + Arrow Keys: Navigate between panes in the specified direction.
Prefix + x: Kill (close) the active pane.
Prefix + z: Toggle Zoom (maximize the active pane; press again to minimize back).

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
4. Customizing Tmux
You can customize Tmux configuration by editing the ~/.tmux.conf file. A popular customization is changing the prefix key to Ctrl+a (similar to GNU Screen) and enabling mouse support.
Create or edit your config:
nano ~/.tmux.conf
Add these lines to configure mouse support and custom keybindings:
# Enable mouse click, scroll, and resize support
set -g mouse on

# Remap prefix from 'Ctrl-b' to 'Ctrl-a'
unbind C-b
set-option -g prefix C-a
bind-option C-a send-prefix

# Split panes using | and - instead of % and "
bind | split-window -h
bind - split-window -v
unbind '"'
unbind %

# Improve status bar styling
set -g status-bg black
set -g status-fg white
Apply your changes immediately without restarting Tmux:
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
In our Linux Desktop Guide, we introduced Hyprland as a dynamic tiling Wayland compositor. Unlike traditional desktop environments, Hyprland is configured entirely via plain text files, allowing you to control layouts, windows, animations, and system scripts directly.
In this guide, we will look at how Hyprland’s configuration works, explain tiling resize commands, understand hyprctl, and implement a custom setup to limit your desktop to exactly 10 persistent workspaces using a shell wrapper script.

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
1. Modular Configuration Structure
A clean Hyprland setup (like the Illogical Impulse repository) splits configurations into multiple modular files sourced by the main configuration file:
# --- ~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf ---

# Source external configuration modules
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/general.conf
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/rules.conf

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
2. Deciphering Keybinds and Dispatchers
Keybindings in Hyprland use the bind keyword:
# Syntax: bind = MODIFIERS, KEY, DISPATCHER, ARGUMENTS
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, L, resizeactivetiling, 40
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, H, resizeactivetiling, -40

Breakdown of the command:

$mainMod: Typically mapped to the SUPER key (Windows key).
SHIFT: The secondary modifier key.
L / H: The trigger keys (Right/Left in Vim-like movement).
resizeactivetiling: The dispatcher command. It tells Hyprland to resize the currently active tiled window.
40 / -40: The argument. It resizes the window split border by 40 pixels (positive expands the window, negative shrinks it).

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
3. What does hyprctl reload do?
Hyprland provides a command-line interface called hyprctl to control the compositor dynamically.
When you edit configuration files, you can force the system to apply the changes immediately by running:
hyprctl reload
This reloads the configuration modules from disk in real-time. Unlike restarting a session under X11, your Wayland session remains active: none of your running applications, terminals, or browser tabs are closed.

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
section: 4. Setup: Limiting to Exactly 10 Persistent Workspaces
text:
4. Setup: Limiting to Exactly 10 Persistent Workspaces
By default, Hyprland creates workspaces dynamically on-demand; if you move your mouse wheel, you can cycle into workspace 11, 12, or higher. To achieve a clean, capped setup of exactly 10 workspaces, follow this three-step procedure:

Step 1: Make Workspaces 1–10 Persistent
Add this to your ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/general.conf (or a dedicated configuration file sourced by your main configuration):
workspace = 1, persistent:true
workspace = 2, persistent:true
workspace = 3, persistent:true
workspace = 4, persistent:true
workspace = 5, persistent:true
workspace = 6, persistent:true
workspace = 7, persistent:true
workspace = 8, persistent:true
workspace = 9, persistent:true
workspace = 10, persistent:true
This forces all 10 workspaces to remain active on your taskbars/bars even if they do not contain any open windows.


Step 2: Create a Workspace Cycle Wrapper Script
The default keybindings cycle infinitely using workspace, e+1. To prevent cycling beyond 10, we will write a script to wrap this action.
Create the script directory and file:
mkdir -p ~/.config/hypr/scripts
Create ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh:
#!/bin/bash
# Usage: workspace-cycle.sh next|prev

# Fetch the active workspace ID using hyprctl JSON output
CURRENT=$(hyprctl activeworkspace -j | jq '.id')

# Calculate the target workspace index (bounded between 1 and 10)
if [[ "$1" == "next" ]]; then
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT < 10 ? CURRENT + 1 : 1 ))
else
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT > 1 ? CURRENT - 1 : 10 ))
fi

# Dispatch the transition to the compositor
hyprctl dispatch workspace "$TARGET"
Make the script executable:
chmod +x ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh


Step 3: Replace Binds in keybinds.conf
Open your ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf and comment out the default wheel-cycling lines:
# Comment out legacy infinite cycling:
# bind = $mainMod, mouse_down, workspace, e+1
# bind = $mainMod, mouse_up, workspace, e-1

# Bind to our wrapper script:
bind = $mainMod, mouse_down, exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh next
bind = $mainMod, mouse_up,   exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh prev

# Or bind to keyboard keys (e.g., arrow keys):
bind = $mainMod, right, exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh next
bind = $mainMod, left,  exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh prev


Step 4: Audit and Apply
Verify if any other infinite cycling commands exist in your files:
grep 'workspace,' ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf | grep -v '^#'
Finally, reload the compositor to apply your changes:
hyprctl reload
For a detailed analysis of how this shell cycle script works line-by-line, see the Scripting Fundamentals Guide.

title: JSON Wrangling: Mastering jq and Programmatic Parsing
text:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the lightweight, text-based standard for data exchange on the modern web. From web APIs and configurations to database storage, almost every developer works with JSON daily.
However, viewing, filtering, and parsing JSON can be challenging, especially in shell environments. This guide explains how to master JSON data wrangling using the command-line utility jq, and demonstrates how to parse and serialize JSON programmatically in Python, JavaScript/Node.js, and Rust.


1. What is JSON?
JSON is structured as a collection of key-value pairs (Objects) and ordered lists (Arrays). It supports six primitive and structured types:

String: Unicode characters enclosed in double quotes (e.g., "username").
Number: Double-precision float (e.g., 42 or 3.1415).
Boolean: true or false.
Null: Represents an empty value (null).
Object: An unordered set of key-value pairs wrapped in curly braces ({}).
Array: An ordered collection of values wrapped in brackets ([]).

Example JSON structure (data.json):
{
  "project": "quarto-writing",
  "active": true,
  "stars": 128,
  "maintainers": [
    {"name": "Igor", "role": "Lead"},
    {"name": "Sarah", "role": "Contributor"}
  ],
  "config": {
    "port": 8080,
    "env": "production"
  }
}



2. Command-Line Processing with jq
jq is a lightweight, flexible command-line JSON processor. It functions like sed or awk but is specifically designed to understand JSON hierarchies.

Pretty Printing and Identity
The simplest filter is ., which takes the input and prints it back as formatted (pretty-printed), colorized JSON:
jq . data.json


Extracting Key Values
You can reference keys using dot-notation:
# Get the project name
jq '.project' data.json  # Output: "quarto-writing"

# Get the port inside the config object
jq '.config.port' data.json  # Output: 8080


Extracting Raw Strings (-r or --raw-output)
By default, jq outputs valid JSON (meaning strings are enclosed in double quotes). To output the raw text directly (ideal for storing in shell variables), use the -r flag:
PROJECT=$(jq -r '.project' data.json)
echo "Deploying $PROJECT..."


Iterating Over Arrays
Use .[] to extract elements from an array:
# Print each maintainer object
jq '.maintainers[]' data.json

# Print only the names of all maintainers
jq '.maintainers[].name' data.json
# Output:
# "Igor"
# "Sarah"


Filtering and Selection (select)
You can use conditionals to filter elements out of an array:
# Example JSON array of users
# [{"name": "Alice", "age": 22}, {"name": "Bob", "age": 30}]
cat users.json | jq '.[] | select(.age >= 25)'
# Output: {"name": "Bob", "age": 30}


Creating New Shapes (Object Reconstruction)
You can map elements into completely new JSON shapes:
jq '.maintainers[] | {user: .name, is_lead: (.role == "Lead")}' data.json
# Output:
# { "user": "Igor", "is_lead": true }
# { "user": "Sarah", "is_lead": false }




3. Programmatic JSON Parsing by Language
While jq is excellent for shell scripts and quick investigations, production applications parse JSON programmatically. Here is how three major languages handle it:

Python (json module)
Python has built-in support for JSON, parsing it directly into standard dictionary and list types.
import json

# JSON String
json_string = '{"name": "Igor", "age": 30, "languages": ["Python", "Rust"]}'

# 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> Python dict)
data = json.loads(json_string)
print(f"Name: {data['name']}, Primary Language: {data['languages'][0]}")

# Modify dict
data["active"] = True

# 2. Serialize (Python dict -> JSON string)
updated_json_string = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(updated_json_string)


JavaScript / Node.js
JSON is natively integrated into JavaScript, sharing syntax directly with JS objects.
// JSON String
const jsonString = '{"name": "Sarah", "role": "Contributor", "stars": 5}';

// 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> JS Object)
const data = JSON.parse(jsonString);
console.log(`User: ${data.name}, Role: ${data.role}`);

// Modify Object
data.stars += 1;

// 2. Serialize (JS Object -> JSON string)
const updatedJsonString = JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
console.log(updatedJsonString);


Rust (serde and serde_json crates)
Rust enforces type safety. The industry standard is serde (Serialization/Deserialization), which compiles fast, type-safe structures mapping directly to JSON.
In Cargo.toml:
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
In main.rs:
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
    languages: Vec<String>,
}

fn main() {
    let json_data = r#"
        {
            "name": "Igor",
            "age": 30,
            "languages": ["Rust", "Python"]
        }
    "#;

    // 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> Rust Struct)
    let user: User = serde_json::from_str(json_data).unwrap();
    println!("Parsed Struct: {:?}", user);
    println!("User Name: {}", user.name);

    // 2. Serialize (Rust Struct -> JSON string)
    let serialized = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&user).unwrap();
    println!("Serialized JSON:\n{}", serialized);
}




4. Conclusion & Quick Reference
For developers, standardizing tools and habits around JSON increases efficiency: * Use jq in terminal pipes to inspect API returns (curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/igor-kan/quarto-writing | jq .stars_count). * Use json.loads/json.dumps in Python for quick scripting. * Define strict structs with serde in Rust to enforce data integrity.

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
Hyprland is a dynamically evolving Wayland compositor. Because it is under active development, its configuration API updates frequently. New versions often deprecate or reorganize configuration options, which can lead to startup warnings, errors, or broken keybinds in popular community configuration presets like Illogical Impulse or other custom rices.
In this guide, we will break down several major breaking changes in recent Hyprland releases, explain what the removed or modified options did, and show you how to patch your configuration files.

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
section: 1. The Removal of misc:vfr (Variable Frame Rate)
text:
1. The Removal of misc:vfr (Variable Frame Rate)
In older versions of Hyprland, you would commonly see this line in general.conf or hyprland.conf:
misc {
    vfr = true
}

What did VFR do?
VFR (Variable Frame Rate) allows the display compositor to pause rendering when nothing on the screen is moving or changing. Instead of constantly drawing 60, 120, or 144 frames per second (which consumes GPU cycles and battery power), the compositor only refreshes the screen when there is movement (e.g., cursor motion, video playback, typing).


The Change
Hyprland has completely integrated and automated frame timing. As a result, the vfr configuration parameter was removed from the misc {} block entirely. If you have vfr = true or vfr = false in your configuration, Hyprland will output a red warning bar on startup:

[Config Error] No such field: vfr



The Fix
Simply remove the vfr line from your config file, or comment it out:
misc {
    # vfr = true # Deprecated: Hyprland handles VFR automatically now
}

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
2. Reorganization of Shadows (decoration:shadow:ignore_window)
Historically, window shadows were defined directly inside the decoration {} block:
decoration {
    drop_shadow = true
    shadow_range = 4
    shadow_render_power = 3
    col.shadow = rgba(1a1a1aee)
    
    # Deprecated path:
    ignore_window = true 
}

What did ignore_window do?
This option controls how shadows are drawn under semi-transparent windows. * When set to true, the shadow is only rendered around the borders of the window, not underneath it. This prevents the shadow from bleeding through a transparent terminal or application, which would make the background look muddy.


The Change
To organize the growing number of shadow parameters, Hyprland moved all shadow configurations into their own sub-block: decoration:shadow {}. Placing ignore_window directly inside decoration {} now throws configuration errors.


The Fix
Nest the shadow parameters inside a dedicated shadow block:
decoration {
    # Other decoration properties like blur, rounding...

    shadow {
        enabled = true
        range = 4
        render_power = 3
        color = rgba(1a1a1aee)
        ignore_window = true # Correct location
    }
}

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
3. Removal of the splitratio Dispatcher
Keybindings in older dotfiles often contained bindings like:
bind = $mainMod, R, splitratio, 0.3

What did splitratio do?
In tiling layouts (like Dwindle or Master), the screen is split between active windows. The splitratio dispatcher allowed you to manually change the dividing ratio of the split window by a specific ratio value, shrinking or expanding the active window relative to its neighbor.


The Change
The splitratio dispatcher was removed. Hyprland now handles active window resizing using more robust dispatchers such as resizeactive or resizeactivetiling.


The Fix
Update your resize keybindings to utilize resizeactive or resizeactivetiling (which take pixel offsets rather than percentage ratios):
# Move split border right (expand active)
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, L, resizeactive, 40 0

# Move split border left (shrink active)
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, H, resizeactive, -40 0

title: Demystifying SQL: Core Concepts, Dialects, and Database Engines
text:
In the landscape of modern software, data is one of the most critical assets. To organize, store, and retrieve this data efficiently, relational database management systems (RDBMS) have been the industry standard for over four decades.
At the center of these systems lies SQL (Structured Query Language). This guide details SQL’s architecture, sub-languages, core operations, and the key differences between popular database engines.


1. What is SQL?
SQL is a declarative programming language designed for managing data held in a Relational Database Management System (RDBMS).
Unlike imperative programming (where you write code detailing how to perform a task), SQL is declarative: you specify what data you want, and the database engine’s query optimizer decides the most efficient way (e.g., using indexes or table scans) to retrieve it.
In a relational database: * Data is stored in Tables (Relations). * Tables consist of Rows (Records) and Columns (Attributes). * Tables are linked together using Primary Keys (unique identifiers) and Foreign Keys (references to primary keys in other tables).



2. The Four SQL Sub-Languages
SQL is divided into four distinct sub-languages, categorized by what the commands do:
mindmap
  root((SQL Commands))
    DDL - Structure
      CREATE
      ALTER
      DROP
      TRUNCATE
    DML - Data
      SELECT
      INSERT
      UPDATE
      DELETE
    DCL - Permissions
      GRANT
      REVOKE
    TCL - Transactions
      COMMIT
      ROLLBACK
      SAVEPOINT

A. DDL (Data Definition Language)
Used to define or modify the database schema and structure (tables, indexes, constraints). * CREATE: Creates tables or databases. * ALTER: Modifies an existing table structure. * DROP: Deletes tables or databases completely. * TRUNCATE: Empties all data inside a table but preserves the structure.


B. DML (Data Manipulation Language)
Used to query, insert, modify, and delete the actual records stored in tables. * SELECT: Retrieves data from one or more tables. * INSERT: Adds new rows. * UPDATE: Modifies existing rows. * DELETE: Removes rows.


C. DCL (Data Control Language)
Used to manage user permissions, security, and access controls. * GRANT: Gives a user access privileges. * REVOKE: Withdraws access privileges.


D. TCL (Transaction Control Language)
Used to manage transactions, ensuring data integrity via ACID properties. * COMMIT: Saves all modifications made during the transaction permanently. * ROLLBACK: Restores the database to its state before the transaction began. * SAVEPOINT: Creates temporary checkpoints within a transaction to roll back to if needed.




3. Core SQL Operations (with Examples)
Here is a typical database scenario containing two tables: users and orders.

Table Creation (DDL)
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT REFERENCES users(id),
    amount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    order_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);


Inserting Records (DML)
INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES 
('Alice Smith', 'alice@example.com'),
('Bob Jones', 'bob@example.com');

INSERT INTO orders (user_id, amount) VALUES 
(1, 49.99),
(1, 150.00),
(2, 22.50);


Querying with Joins (DML)
To combine columns from both tables, we use a JOIN:
SELECT users.name, orders.amount, orders.order_date
FROM users
INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id
WHERE orders.amount > 30.00
ORDER BY orders.amount DESC;


Grouping and Aggregating Data
To find the total amount spent by each user:
SELECT users.name, SUM(orders.amount) AS total_spent
FROM users
LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id
GROUP BY users.name
HAVING SUM(orders.amount) > 50.00;




4. Comparing SQL Dialects and Database Engines
Although SQL is standardized by ANSI/ISO, every major database engine implements its own features, syntax adjustments, and extensions (known as dialects).

A. PostgreSQL

Type: Open-source Object-Relational Database.
Key Features: Highly extensible, supports advanced indexing, JSON querying natively, window functions, and custom data types.
Best For: Complex applications, GIS data tracking (via PostGIS), and enterprise-grade reliability.



B. MySQL / MariaDB

Type: Open-source Relational Database.
Key Features: Extremely fast read performance, simple to set up, highly popular in web hosting environments (LAMP stack).
Best For: Web applications, content management systems (like WordPress), and standard CRUD applications.



C. SQLite

Type: Serverless, embedded file-based database.
Key Features: Extremely lightweight. The entire database is stored in a single file on disk. No server configuration required.
Best For: Local application testing, mobile applications (iOS/Android), and local CLI utilities.



D. Microsoft SQL Server / Oracle Database

Type: Commercial proprietary databases.
Key Features: High-end security integration, advanced query optimization, robust commercial support.
Best For: Large-scale enterprise systems and financial processing software.





5. Summary: SQL vs. NoSQL








Feature
Relational (SQL)
Non-Relational (NoSQL)




Data Model
Tabular (Rows/Columns)
Document (JSON), Key-Value, Graph


Schema
Strict, predefined
Dynamic, flexible


Transactions
Strict compliance (ACID)
Eventual consistency (BASE)


Scaling
Vertical (Larger server)
Horizontal (More servers)


Use Case
Financial applications, complex joins
Big data, real-time analytics, user profiles

title: Scripting Fundamentals: Understanding Bash Syntax & Positional Arguments
text:
In modern operating systems, automation is built on scripts. A script is simply a plain text file containing a sequence of commands that are executed by an interpreter (such as Bash, Python, or Node.js).
A wrapper script is a specific type of script that wraps around an existing program or command to inject extra logic, handle default options, validate parameters, or filter output before executing the main application.
In this guide, we will look at the step-by-step workflow for creating scripts on Linux and analyze a functional workspace cycling script line-by-line to master shell syntax.

title: Scripting Fundamentals: Understanding Bash Syntax & Positional Arguments
text:
1. The Script Creation Workflow
To create and run any custom script in Linux, you follow a standard three-step workflow:

Step A: Create the Directory
Use mkdir -p to safely create the destination directory. The -p (parents) flag ensures that no error is thrown if the directory already exists, and it creates any missing parent folders along the path.
mkdir -p ~/.config/hypr/scripts


Step B: Write the Script File
You can write the file using a terminal editor, or use a Here-Document (Here-Doc) redirection command in your terminal.
The syntax cat > filename << 'EOF' redirects everything you type next into filename until it encounters the string EOF. Putting single quotes around 'EOF' is critical: it prevents your current terminal session from expanding variables (like $1 or $CURRENT) while writing the file, leaving the code intact for the script to execute later.
cat > ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Usage: workspace-cycle.sh next|prev
CURRENT=$(hyprctl activeworkspace -j | jq '.id')
if [[ "$1" == "next" ]]; then
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT < 10 ? CURRENT + 1 : 1 ))
else
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT > 1 ? CURRENT - 1 : 10 ))
fi
hyprctl dispatch workspace "$TARGET"
EOF


Step C: Grant Execution Permissions
By default, new files on Linux do not have permission to run as programs. You must change the file mode using chmod +x (change mode + execute):
chmod +x ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh

title: Scripting Fundamentals: Understanding Bash Syntax & Positional Arguments
text:
2. Line-by-Line Code Analysis
Let’s dissect the contents of the workspace-cycle.sh script to understand every keyword and operator used in Bash:
#!/bin/bash

The Shebang: The first line of any shell script. The #! sequence tells the operating system kernel to load the /bin/bash binary to interpret and run the rest of the commands in the file.

CURRENT=$(hyprctl activeworkspace -j | jq '.id')

Command Substitution $(...): Runs the commands inside the parentheses and assigns their standard output (stdout) directly to the variable CURRENT.
JSON Output hyprctl activeworkspace -j: Calls Hyprland’s control utility, requesting information about the currently focused workspace in JSON format (e.g., {"id": 3, "name": "3", "windows": 2}).
Piping to jq: The pipe operator | passes the JSON output to jq (a command-line JSON processor). The query '.id' extracts the value of the “id” key (e.g., 3) and strips any outer quotes.

if [[ "$1" == "next" ]]; then

Positional Arguments $1: When you run a script, any parameters you type after the script name are passed as positional variables. $1 is the first parameter (e.g., next in ./workspace-cycle.sh next), $2 is the second, and so on.
Double Brackets [[ ... ]]: The standard modern Bash test operator, used to evaluate conditions.
Comparison ==: Checks if the value of the first argument equals the string "next".

    TARGET=$(( CURRENT < 10 ? CURRENT + 1 : 1 ))

Arithmetic Expansion $(( ... )): Performs integer mathematical operations.
Ternary Operator condition ? true_val : false_val:

If the value of CURRENT is less than 10, it evaluates to CURRENT + 1 (advancing to the next workspace).
If CURRENT is 10, it evaluates to 1 (wrapping around to the first workspace).
This prevents the workspace index from exceeding our target cap of 10.


else
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT > 1 ? CURRENT - 1 : 10 ))
fi

Reverse Cycling: If the argument passed is not "next" (meaning it is "prev"), this decrement condition is triggered.

If CURRENT is greater than 1, it shifts to CURRENT - 1.
If CURRENT is 1, it wraps around to 10.

fi: The closing keyword for if statements in Bash (simply “if” spelled backward).

hyprctl dispatch workspace "$TARGET"

Dispatcher Command: Executes the compositor dispatcher command to switch focus directly to the target workspace ID resolved by the script (e.g., hyprctl dispatch workspace 4).

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
For users transitioning to Linux or diving deeper into system customization (“ricing”), the visual layer of the operating system can seem like a confusing maze of acronyms and interchangeable terms.
Unlike Windows or macOS, where the graphical user interface (GUI) is tightly coupled with the core operating system, Linux treats the GUI as a modular, replaceable stack of software. This article breaks down the entire desktop stack from display protocols to custom rices like Illogical Impulse, complete with installation commands, configuration paths, and configuration examples.

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
1. The Foundation: Display Protocols & Servers
At the very bottom of the graphical stack sits the Display Server. Its job is to coordinate communication between your hardware (graphics card, keyboard, mouse) and your applications, telling the hardware where and how to render pixels.
Here is how data flows through the Linux graphical stack:



Linux Desktop Stack Architecture




Click to view Mermaid Diagram Code

flowchart TD
    subgraph InputOutput [Hardware Layer]
        Hardware["Hardware (GPU, Keyboard, Mouse)"]
    end
    subgraph ProtocolLayer [Display Server Protocol]
        DisplayServer["Display Server (Xorg / Wayland Compositor)"]
    end
    subgraph WindowLayer [Window Management Layer]
        WindowManager["Window Manager / Compositor (Mutter, KWin, Hyprland, i3)"]
    end
    subgraph AppLayer [User Space Applications]
        Client["GUI Applications (Firefox, Kitty, Files)"]
    end

    Hardware -->|Input Events| DisplayServer
    DisplayServer -->|Display Signals| Hardware
    Client -->|Render Commands| WindowManager
    WindowManager -->|Composed Frames| DisplayServer
    DisplayServer -->|Input Events Routing| Client


X11 (X Window System)
Introduced in 1984, the X Window System (specifically its modern server implementation, Xorg) is the legacy standard. * How it works: It uses a client-server architecture. Applications (clients) send drawing requests to the X Server, which interacts with the hardware. A separate Window Manager is responsible for arranging the application windows. * Network Transparency: X11 natively supports running an application on a remote server and displaying its window on your local machine. * Downsides: It is old, bloated, lacks built-in security isolation (any app can capture keystrokes from other apps), and is prone to screen tearing.


Wayland
Wayland is the modern successor to X11, designed to simplify the stack and enhance performance and security. * How it works: Wayland is a protocol, not a server. The server is called a Wayland Compositor (which acts as the display server, window manager, and compositor all in one). * Direct Rendering: Applications render directly into their own off-screen buffers, and the compositor paints them to the screen. Every frame is perfect (no screen tearing). * Security: Strict isolation. Applications cannot sniff keystrokes or record screens without explicit permission through system portals.

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
2. Window Managers (WM) vs. Desktop Environments (DE)
When you interact with panels, menus, and window frames, you are interacting with either a Window Manager or a full Desktop Environment.



Component
Purpose
Resource Usage
Examples




Window Manager (WM)
Solitary job: positioning, sizing, and styling application windows.
Extremely low (~50MB - 150MB RAM)
i3wm, bspwm, Hyprland, Sway


Desktop Environment (DE)
A complete suite of unified applications (file manager, settings, panels, system tray, display manager, WM).
Moderate to High (500MB - 2GB+ RAM)
GNOME, KDE Plasma, XFCE




Desktop Environments

GNOME
Built on the GTK toolkit, GNOME focuses on a distraction-free, touch-friendly, workspace-centric interface. It defaults to Wayland and uses its own compositor called Mutter.


KDE Plasma
Built on Qt, KDE Plasma is famous for being incredibly modular and customizable. It is lightweight despite its power and supports both X11 and Wayland via its compositor/WM, KWin.


XFCE4
A lightweight DE built on GTK. XFCE is modular, stable, and uses very little RAM, making it perfect for older hardware. It operates primarily on X11 using the Xfwm window manager.




Window Managers & Compositors

Hyprland
Hyprland is a dynamic tiling Wayland compositor written in C++. It is popular for its fluid animations, rounded corners, dual-gaps, active blur rendering, and extensive customizability.


i3wm
i3wm is a classic, manual tiling window manager for X11. It organizes windows in a non-overlapping grid, heavily relying on keyboard shortcuts.

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
3. What are Dotfiles?
In Linux, user-specific configurations are stored as plain text files, often prefixed with a dot (.), which hides them in standard directory listings. Collectively, these are known as dotfiles.

Standard Locations

Global config folder: ~/.config/ (contains configuration folders for most modern applications).
Shell configurations: ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc (stored directly in the home directory).
X11 Startup: ~/.xinitrc (scripts executed when launching X11).



Illogical Impulse: Next-Gen Hyprland Config
Illogical Impulse (developed by GitHub user end-4) is a highly integrated, aesthetic, and usability-first set of dotfiles for the Hyprland Wayland compositor. * Core Technology: It relies heavily on Quickshell (and previously AGS - Aylur’s GTK Shell) to construct widgets, control hubs, volume sliders, app launchers, and status bars using Javascript/Typescript. * Why it’s unique: Unlike traditional configs where you chain different tools together (e.g., Waybar for status bar, Rofi for launcher, Dunst for notifications), Illogical Impulse unifies all desktop components into a single, cohesive Material Design interface.

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
4. Installation & Setup Guide

Installing the Graphics Stack
Below are commands to install different desktop options on Arch Linux and Ubuntu/Debian:

Installing DEs:
# Arch Linux
sudo pacman -S gnome                 # GNOME Group
sudo pacman -S plasma-meta kde-applications # KDE Plasma Suite
sudo pacman -S xfce4 xfce4-goodies   # XFCE4

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install ubuntu-desktop      # GNOME (Default Ubuntu)
sudo apt install kde-standard        # KDE Plasma
sudo apt install xfce4 xfce4-goodies # XFCE4


Installing Hyprland (Wayland WM):
# Arch Linux (Recommended)
sudo pacman -S hyprland waybar kitty rofi-wayland dunst polkit-kde-agent

# Ubuntu (Requires 23.04 or newer)
sudo apt install hyprland



Deploying the “Illogical Impulse” Dotfiles
To deploy the custom Illogical Impulse desktop environment, you should use the official installation script on an Arch-based system:
# Clone the repository
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/end-4/dots-hyprland.git ~/dots-hyprland

# Navigate and run the installation script
cd ~/dots-hyprland
./install.sh
Note: Make sure to read the installer prompts carefully, as it manages system packages and backup files.

title: Demystifying the Linux Desktop Architecture
text:
5. Configuration & Structure Examples
Here is how configuration files for various components are structured and where they are placed.

Hyprland Configuration
Path: ~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf
# --- Example hyprland.conf snippet ---

# Monitor Configuration
monitor=DP-1, 1920x1080@144, 0x0, 1

# Auto-start essential applications
exec-once = waybar & dunst & hyprpaper

# Styling
general {
    gaps_in = 5
    gaps_out = 10
    border_size = 2
    col.active_border = rgba(33ccffee) rgba(00ff99ee) 45deg
    col.inactive_border = rgba(595959aa)
    layout = dwindle
}

decoration {
    rounding = 10
    blur {
        enabled = true
        size = 8
        passes = 2
    }
}

# Keybindings
$mainMod = SUPER
bind = $mainMod, Q, exec, kitty
bind = $mainMod, C, killactive, 
bind = $mainMod, M, exit, 
bind = $mainMod, V, togglefloating, 
bind = $mainMod, left, movefocus, l
bind = $mainMod, right, movefocus, r


X11 i3wm Configuration
Path: ~/.config/i3/config
# --- Example i3 config snippet ---

# Modifier Key (Alt = Mod1, Super/Windows = Mod4)
set $mod Mod4

# Font configuration
font pango:DejaVu Sans Mono 8

# Keyboard bindings to launch applications
bindsym $mod+Return exec i3-sensible-terminal
bindsym $mod+d exec dmenu_run

# Kill focused window
bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill

# Split direction keys
bindsym $mod+h split h
bindsym $mod+v split v


How WMs launch from terminal: .xinitrc
For X11 Window Managers, you control how the session starts using your ~/.xinitrc file:
# --- ~/.xinitrc ---

# Start background services
feh --bg-scale ~/Pictures/wallpaper.png &
picom --experimental-backends &  # Compositor for rounded corners/blur under X11
dunst &                          # Notification daemon

# Execute the Window Manager (Must remain in foreground)
exec i3
For Wayland, sessions are usually started directly from a display manager (like SDDM or GDM) or by executing the compositor command directly from the TTY console:
Hyprland

title: Understanding the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
text:
For users coming from Windows, the Linux filesystem can seem disorienting. Windows organizes files around physical storage drives (e.g., C:\ for the primary system, D:\ for external drives).
Linux, however, structures everything under a single unified directory tree starting from the Root directory (/). Physical storage devices are “mounted” to specific directories within this single tree.
This structure is governed by the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), ensuring consistency across different Linux distributions.

title: Understanding the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
text:
1. The FHS Directory Tree
Here is a visual map of the standard Linux filesystem structure:
flowchart TD
    Root["/ (Root)"] --> bin["/bin (Essential User Binaries)"]
    Root --> boot["/boot (Kernel & Bootloader)"]
    Root --> dev["/dev (Device Files)"]
    Root --> etc["/etc (System Configuration Files)"]
    Root --> home["/home (User Home Directories)"]
    Root --> lib["/lib (Shared Libraries)"]
    Root --> opt["/opt (Optional Software Packages)"]
    Root --> proc["/proc (Virtual Process Filesystem)"]
    Root --> rootDir["/root (Superuser Home Directory)"]
    Root --> tmp["/tmp (Temporary Files)"]
    Root --> usr["/usr (User Utilities)"]
    Root --> var["/var (Variable Data Logs)"]

    usr --> usrBin["/usr/bin (Non-essential Binaries)"]
    usr --> usrShare["/usr/share (Shared App Data)"]
    var --> varLog["/var/log (System Logs)"]

title: Understanding the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
text:
2. Directory Breakdown & Purpose

/ (Root)
The primary directory that contains all other directories and files on the system, regardless of which physical disk partition they reside on.


/bin and /sbin

/bin (Binaries): Essential command-line utilities needed in single-user mode or for system repair (e.g., ls, cp, bash).
/sbin (System Binaries): Essential system administration commands reserved for the superuser (e.g., iptables, fdisk, reboot).
Note: In modern distributions, /bin and /sbin are often symbolic links to /usr/bin and /usr/sbin.



/boot
Contains the static files needed to start the operating system, including the Linux kernel, initial RAM disk (initramfs), and bootloader configuration (GRUB).


/dev (Devices)
In Unix/Linux, “everything is a file”. This directory contains virtual files representing physical hardware. For example: * /dev/sda represents the first hard disk drive. * /dev/input/mice represents mouse input. * /dev/null is a virtual device that discards all data written to it.


/etc (Editable Text Configuration)
The nerve center of system configuration. It contains host-specific configuration files for the operating system and services. For example: * /etc/passwd lists local system users. * /etc/hosts configures hostname-to-IP mappings. * /etc/fstab defines disk mounting points.


/home and /root

/home: Contains the home directories for standard users (e.g., /home/igorkan). This is where files, desktop folders, and user configuration dotfiles (~/.config/) reside.
/root: The home directory for the superuser/administrator (root). It is separated from /home to ensure the system administrator can still log in and repair the machine even if the /home partition fails to mount.



/proc and /sys (Virtual Filesystems)
These are not real folders on your hard drive; they are virtual interfaces created by the Linux kernel. * /proc (Process): Contains files representing running processes and kernel parameters. For instance, reading /proc/cpuinfo displays CPU specifications. * /sys (System): Provides hierarchical information about hardware drivers and kernel subsystems.


/usr (User System Resources)
Contains user utilities, libraries, and documentation. * /usr/bin contains non-essential executables (like python, git, and nodejs). * /usr/lib holds shared library binaries. * /usr/share holds architecture-independent files like icons, themes, and documentation.


/var (Variable)
Stores data that changes dynamically as the system operates. * /var/log contains system and application log files (e.g., syslog, boot logs). * /var/spool holds print queues and mail queues. * /var/cache holds cached application data.


/tmp (Temporary)
A scratch directory where applications can read and write temporary files. Typically, the files here are cleared automatically every time the computer reboots.

title: Formal Rules of Syntactic Implication
text:
Syntactic implication utilizes deductive inference rules to transform premise sets into target conclusions. In what is also called a Sequent-style Calculus or Natural Deduction framework, let \(\Gamma\) represent a set of formulas acting as premises (a.k.a. hypotheses), let \(\varphi, \psi, \theta\) represent individual formulas, and let the turnstile symbol \(\vdash\) denote “syntactically derives.”

Basic Proofs (Axioms)
These foundational rules establish the starting points for any formal derivation.

Assumption (\(Assume_{\mathcal{L}}\)): If a formula is already present within your active set of hypotheses, it is derived trivially.
\[\Gamma \vdash \varphi \quad \text{if } \varphi \in \Gamma\]
Equality Reflexivity (\(EqRefl\)): Every valid term is inherently equal to itself.
\[\Gamma \vdash t = t \quad \text{for all } t \in \text{Term}_{\mathcal{L}}\]



Proof Rules (Connectives)
These inference rules dictate how to introduce new logical connectives into a derivation or eliminate existing ones to extract substructures.

Conjunction

Elimination (\(\wedge EL\) and \(\wedge ER\)): If a compound conjunction is derived, either constituent proposition can be extracted individually.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \psi}\]
Introduction (\(\wedge I\)): If independent derivations exist for two separate formulas, they can be unified into a single conjunction.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \quad \Gamma \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}\]



Disjunction

Introduction (\(\vee IL\) and \(\vee IR\)): If a formula is derived, it can be disjoined with any arbitrary proposition while preserving validity.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \vee \psi} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\Gamma \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \vee \psi}\]
Proof by Cases (\(\vee PC\)): If two distinct hypotheses independently derive the identical consequent \(\theta\), then the disjunction of those hypotheses also derives \(\theta\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\} \vdash \theta \quad \Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \theta}{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi \vee \psi\} \vdash \theta}\]



Implication

Elimination / Modus Ponens (\(\to E\)): If a conditional implication and its operational antecedent are both derived, the consequent necessarily follows.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi \quad \Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \psi}\]
Introduction / Deduction Theorem (\(\to I\)): If assuming a provisional hypothesis successfully derives a target formula, the overarching implication is established.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\} \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi}\]



Negation and Contradiction

Proof by Contradiction (\(\neg PC\)): If assuming a hypothesis yields a structural contradiction (deriving both a formula and its explicit negation), the hypothesis is refuted.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \varphi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \neg \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \neg \psi}\]
Contradiction Rule / Reductio ad Absurdum (\(Contr\)): If assuming the negation of a proposition yields a logical contradiction, the foundational proposition is affirmed as true.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\neg \varphi\} \vdash \psi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\neg \varphi\} \vdash \neg \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}\]




Equality Rules

Substitution (\(=Sub\)): If a formula holds true for a specific term \(t\), and an explicit identity mapping establishes that \(t\) equals \(u\), the formula remains valid when \(t\) is replaced by \(u\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t \quad \Gamma \vdash t = u}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_u}\]



Quantifier Rules
Quantifier rules govern the systematic introduction and elimination of operational scope variables across domains.

Existential Quantifiers

Introduction (\(\exists I\)): Proving that a specific instantiated term satisfies a target property confirms that there exists at least one element satisfying that property.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t}{\Gamma \vdash \exists x \, \varphi}\]
Existential Elimination / Proof (\(\exists P\)): If an arbitrary placeholder \(y\) can derive a conclusion \(\psi\) from an existential statement, the derivation holds universally, provided \(y\) remains unbound within the surrounding context.
\[\Gamma \cup \{\varphi^x_y\} \vdash \psi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\exists x \, \varphi\} \vdash \psi \quad \text{if } y \notin \text{FreeVar}(\Gamma \cup \{\exists x \, \varphi, \psi\})\]



Universal Quantifiers

Elimination (\(\forall E\)): If a property is universally quantified across an entire domain, it holds valid for any specific instantiated term \(t\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \forall x \, \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t}\]
Introduction (\(\forall I\)): If a property can be derived for a completely arbitrary, unconstrained placeholder \(y\), it is formally established for all elements in the domain.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_y}{\Gamma \vdash \forall x \, \varphi} \quad \text{if } y \notin \text{FreeVar}(\Gamma \cup \{\forall x \, \varphi\})\]




Superset Rule

Monotonicity (\(Super\)): Classical deduction is monotonic. Adding supplementary hypotheses to a valid derivation context never invalidates the previously established conclusion.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma' \vdash \varphi} \quad \text{if } \Gamma' \supseteq \Gamma\]

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
In English, how we ask questions says a lot about our relationship with the listener, the context of the conversation, and our level of politeness.
Compare these two queries: 1. “Where is the bathroom?” 2. “Could you tell me where the bathroom is?”
While both seek the exact same information, the first is a direct question, which can sound abrupt or demanding, especially when speaking to strangers. The second is an indirect question, which softens the request by embedding the question inside a polite introductory phrase.
For English learners, mastering indirect questions is one of the most critical milestones for achieving professional fluency. For native speakers, understanding the subtle syntax of embedded clauses prevents hypercorrections and enhances stylistic clarity.
This guide provides a comprehensive breakdown of direct and indirect questions, highlighting structural rules, tense shifts, punctuation, and advanced stylistic nuances.

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
1. Grammatical Framework: The Golden Rules
When transforming a direct question into an indirect question, you must follow three fundamental grammatical changes.

Rule 1: Use Statement Word Order (No Subject-Verb Inversion)
In direct questions, the subject and the verb are inverted (the verb or auxiliary comes before the subject). In indirect questions, we revert to standard declarative (statement) word order: Subject + Verb.

Direct: Where is (verb) the station (subject)?
Indirect: Can you tell me where the station (subject) is (verb)?

(Incorrect: Can you tell me where is the station?)

Direct: What time does (auxiliary) the meeting (subject) start?
Indirect: Do you know what time the meeting (subject) starts (verb)?

(Incorrect: Do you know what time does the meeting start?)




Rule 2: Omit Auxiliary Verbs (Do, Does, Did)
In direct questions, we use the auxiliary verbs do, does, or did to form questions in the Simple Present and Simple Past. In indirect questions, these auxiliaries are completely dropped, and the main verb must be conjugated to match the subject and tense.

Direct (Present Simple): Where do you live?
Indirect: Could you tell me where you live? (Not: where do you live)
Direct (Present Simple 3rd Person): What does he want?
Indirect: I wonder what he wants. (Verb conjugated with -s; not: what does he want)
Direct (Past Simple): Why did she leave?
Indirect: I don’t know why she left. (Verb conjugated in past tense; not: why did she leave / why she did leave)



Rule 3: Use If or Whether for Yes/No Questions
If a direct question does not begin with a question word (who, what, where, when, why, how), it is a Yes/No question. To make it indirect, you must introduce the embedded clause using if or whether.

Direct: Is she coming to the party?
Indirect: Do you know if she is coming to the party?
Direct: Did you finish the report?
Indirect: Could you let me know whether you finished the report?

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
2. Comparison Across Verb Tenses & Forms
To illustrate how these rules apply systematically, here is an extensive comparison across major English tenses and modal structures.









Tense / Form
Direct Question
Indirect Question (Polite Opening)
Indirect Question (Statement Opening)




Present Simple

“I am not sure where he is.”

“Could you tell me how often you exercise?”
“I would like to know how often you exercise.”

“Do you have any idea what they are doing?”
“I want to see what they are doing.”

“Where did you buy that?”
“Would you mind telling me where you bought that?”
“He didn’t mention where he bought that.”

“Can you remember who she was talking to?”
“I was wondering who she was talking to.”

“Do you know why they have left?”
“It’s unclear why they have left.”

“Can you tell me what he had prepared?”
“She didn’t disclose what he had prepared.”

“I was wondering when the package will arrive.”

“Could you tell me who you are going to invite?”
“I’m curious who you are going to invite.”


Modal (Should)

“Do you have any advice on what we should do?”
“We need to figure out what we should do.”

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
section: 3. Polite Phrases to Start Indirect Questions
text:
3. Polite Phrases to Start Indirect Questions
The tone of an indirect question is determined by the introductory clause. Here are the most common phrases grouped by usage.

A. Polite Inquiries (Ended with a Question Mark)
Use these when asking a question to a stranger, a colleague, or a customer. * “Could you tell me…” (Very common, polite, and versatile) * “Do you know…” (Slightly more direct, but still polite) * “Do you have any idea…” (Useful when you suspect the person might not know the answer) * “Would you mind telling me…” (Extremely polite; note that if followed by a verb it takes -ing, e.g., “Would you mind telling me what time it is?”) * “Can you remember…” (Used when asking about past events or details)


B. Statement Openings (Ended with a Period)
Use these to express uncertainty, curiosity, or when you are reporting information. * “I was wondering…” (Very soft and polite, commonly used in emails) * “I’d like to know…” (Professional and clear, shows intent) * “I’m not sure…” (Expresses doubt or lack of information) * “I don’t know…” (Simple statement of fact) * “I want to find out…” (Expresses a goal or objective) * “It is not clear…” (Formal, analytical)

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
4. Nuances: Punctuation and “If” vs. “Whether”
Even advanced speakers make mistakes on these two key areas of indirect question usage.

A. Punctuation Rules
Should an indirect question end with a question mark (?) or a period (.)? The rule depends entirely on the introductory clause:

If the introductory clause is a question, the whole sentence ends with a question mark.

Do you know (question) where he lives?
Could you tell me (question) if it’s raining?

If the introductory clause is a statement, the whole sentence ends with a period.

I was wondering (statement) where he lives.
I’d like to know (statement) if it’s raining.




B. If vs. Whether
While if and whether are interchangeable in most yes/no indirect questions, there are subtle differences:

Use “whether” in formal writing: It sounds more professional and academic.

Formal: “The board must decide whether to approve the budget.”

Use “whether” when presenting two explicit options (especially with “or not”):

“I don’t know whether they will accept the offer or not.”
“Could you tell me whether he is arriving by train or plane?”

Use “whether” immediately before an infinitive (to + verb):

“She was debating whether to buy the house.” (You cannot say “if to buy”)

Use “whether” after prepositions:

“We had a discussion about whether we should relocate.” (You cannot say “about if we should”)

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
section: 5. Advanced Stylistic & Syntactic Analyses (For Native & Advanced Speakers)
text:
5. Advanced Stylistic & Syntactic Analyses (For Native & Advanced Speakers)
For fluent and native speakers, indirect questions present interesting syntactic structures, reported speech rules, and common errors to avoid.

A. Fronted Wh-Words vs. Embedded Questions
Consider the difference between these two constructions involving opinion verbs (like think, believe, suppose):

Embedded Wh-clause: “Do you know who that candidate is?”

Here, “who that candidate is” is a noun clause serving as the direct object of the verb “know”.

Fronted Wh-word: “Who do you think that candidate is?”

In sentences with verbs of opinion (think, believe, suppose, imagine), the wh-word is extracted from the embedded clause and moved to the front of the entire sentence.
Incorrect: “Do you think who that candidate is?”




B. Indirect Questions in Reported Speech (Backshifting)
When reporting a question that was asked in the past, the tenses in the indirect question must typically shift backward (backshifting):

Original Direct Question: “Where are you going?” (Present Continuous)
Reported Indirect Question: “She asked me where I was going.” (Past Continuous)
Original Yes/No Question: “Did you see the movie?” (Past Simple)
Reported Indirect Question: “He wanted to know if I had seen the movie.” (Past Perfect)



C. Infinitival Indirect Questions
In English, we can shorten indirect questions when the subject of the introductory clause is the same as the subject of the question. We do this by replacing the subject and auxiliary with a to-infinitive:

“I don’t know what I should do.” \(\rightarrow\) “I don’t know what to do.”
“Could you tell me how I can get there?” \(\rightarrow\) “Could you tell me how to get there?”
“She wasn’t sure whether she should go.” \(\rightarrow\) “She wasn’t sure whether to go.”



D. Hypercorrection and Spoken English Deviations
In informal spoken English, native speakers often apply direct question inversion to indirect clauses. While common in casual speech, this is considered ungrammatical in formal writing.

Casual Speech: “He asked me what was I doing.”
Grammatically Correct: “He asked me what I was doing.”
Casual Speech: “I wonder how did they manage to do that.”
Grammatically Correct: “I wonder how they managed to do that.”

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
6. Practice Exercises & Sentence Transformations
Test your skills by rewriting these direct questions into indirect questions.

Exercise 1: Transform to Indirect (Polite Question form)
Example: “Where is the post office?” \(\rightarrow\) “Could you tell me where the post office is?”

“What time does the bank close?” (Use: Do you know…)
“Is there a vegetarian option on the menu?” (Use: Could you tell me…)
“Why did the project fail?” (Use: Do you have any idea…)
“Where can I find a taxi?” (Use: Would you mind showing me…)
“Will it snow tomorrow?” (Use: Do you know…)



Exercise 2: Transform to Indirect (Statement form)
Example: “Why is she upset?” \(\rightarrow\) “I don’t know why she is upset.”

“How did he solve the puzzle?” (Use: I was wondering…)
“Should we sign the contract?” (Use: We need to decide whether…)
“When are they arriving?” (Use: I’m not sure…)
“Did he receive my email?” (Use: I’d like to find out…)
“Where did I leave my keys?” (Use: I can’t remember…)




Answer Key

Exercise 1

Do you know what time the bank closes? (No “does”, conjugated verb)
Could you tell me if/whether there is a vegetarian option on the menu? (Yes/no question uses if/whether)
Do you have any idea why the project failed? (Past tense main verb, no “did”)
Would you mind showing me where I can find a taxi? (Subject “I” before modal “can”)
Do you know if/whether it will snow tomorrow?



Exercise 2

I was wondering how he solved the puzzle. (Ends with a period)
We need to decide whether to sign the contract. (Or: whether we should sign…)
I’m not sure when they are arriving.
I’d like to find out if/whether he received my email.
I can’t remember where I left my keys.

title: Sound in Words: The Ultimate Guide to Onomatopoeia
text:
Have you ever wondered why we say a dog goes “woof”, a bee goes “buzz”, or a clock goes “tick-tock”? These words do not just describe a sound; they are the sound.
This linguistic phenomenon is called onomatopoeia (pronounced /ˌɒnəˌmætəˈpiːə/ or ah-nuh-mah-tuh-PEE-uh). It comes from the Greek words onoma (name) and poiein (to make), literally meaning “word-making” or “name-creation.”
For English learners, onomatopoeia is a fantastic tool to make your writing and speaking sound more natural, expressive, and vivid. For native speakers, it is a key element of creative writing, poetry, comic books, and sound design.
In this guide, we will provide a massive index of examples categorized by type, explain how to use these words grammatically, compare how different languages hear the same sounds, and explore how advanced writers use sound symbolism to elevate their prose.

title: Sound in Words: The Ultimate Guide to Onomatopoeia
text:
1. Categorized Index of Onomatopoeia
To help you navigate the vast landscape of English sound words, we have organized them into six primary categories. Each entry includes its typical meaning and a sentence demonstrating its usage.

A. Animal Sounds
Animals are the most common source of onomatopoeia. Interestingly, these sounds vary wildly between different languages (which we will explore in Section 4).








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Bark / Woof / Arf
Dog barking
“The dog began to bark at the mail carrier.”


Meow / Purr
Cat calling or expressing contentment
“The kitten let out a soft meow and started to purr.”


Oink / Squeal
Pig sounds
“The pigs oinked happily as the farmer filled their trough.”


Quack
Duck sound
“A family of ducks quacked as they swam across the pond.”


Buzz
Bee or flying insect
“A swarm of angry bees began to buzz around the hive.”


Chirp / Tweet
Small bird or cricket
“Birds chirped merrily in the trees on a sunny morning.”


Squeak
Mouse or rusty door hinge
“A mouse squeaked behind the cupboard and ran away.”


Hiss
Snake or escaping steam
“The snake reared its head and let out a menacing hiss.”


Moo
Cow
“The cows mooed in the pasture as the sun went down.”


Neigh / Whinny
Horse
“The stallion gave a loud neigh and galloped away.”


Baa / Bleat
Sheep or goat
“The lost lamb was bleating for its mother in the fog.”


Roar
Lion or large predator
“The lion’s mighty roar echoed across the savanna.”


Crow / Cock-a-doodle-doo
Rooster
“The rooster crowed at dawn, waking up the entire farm.”


Croak
Frog or toad
“Deep in the swamp, frogs croaked through the night.”


Cluck
Hen / chicken
“The hens clucked as they pecked at seed in the dirt.”


Hoot
Owl
“An owl hooted from the depths of the dark forest.”






B. Water and Liquid Sounds
Water is highly dynamic, and English has developed highly specific words to match the different movements and volumes of liquids.








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Splash
An object hitting water
“The child jumped into the pool with a loud splash.”


Drip / Drop
Small, slow water movement
“I couldn’t sleep because of the constant drip of the kitchen faucet.”


Gurgle
Water flowing over rocks or down a drain
“A shallow stream gurgles gently through the backyard.”


Plop
A small, heavy object dropping into liquid
“The ice cube landed in the glass with a quiet plop.”


Slosh
Liquid moving violently in a container
“Water sloshed out of the bucket as I walked up the stairs.”


Squish / Squelch
Walking through wet mud or squeezing something wet
“My boots made a wet squish sound as I walked through the marsh.”


Bubble
Liquid boiling or releasing gas
“The hot soup started to bubble and steam on the stove.”


Fizz / Sizzle
Carbonated drinks or frying food
“You can hear the fizz of the soda when you open the can.”


Splashdown
A spacecraft landing in the ocean
“The capsule completed a successful splashdown in the Pacific.”






C. Collision, Impact, and Explosion Sounds
These words are essential in action writing, comic books, and descriptions of physical movements or accidents.








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Bang
A sudden, loud noise (gunshot, door slamming)
“The door slammed shut with a sudden, deafening bang.”


Boom
A deep, resonant explosion or thunder
“A loud boom shook the windows as lightning struck nearby.”


Crash
Large objects breaking or colliding
“We heard a loud crash and realized a plate had dropped.”


Thud
A dull, heavy object hitting a soft surface
“The heavy textbook fell off the desk and landed with a thud.”


Clank
Metallic objects striking each other
“The metal chains clanked against the side of the ship.”


Slap
Flat contact with a surface
“She gave the tabletop a sharp slap to get everyone’s attention.”


Thwack / Whack
Striking something with a stick or flat object
“The bat hit the baseball with a satisfying thwack.”


Smash
Violent breaking or crushing
“He watched the waves smash against the rocky cliffs.”


Pop
A small, sharp explosion (balloon, popcorn)
“The balloon went pop when it touched the rose bush.”


Clatter
Many hard objects falling and hitting
“The dirty dishes clattered in the kitchen sink.”


Crunch
Crushing something hard or dry (leaves, snow, chips)
“I love the sound of dry leaves crunching under my feet.”


Slam
Closing something with violent force
“Please don’t slam the car door when you get out.”


Crack
Sharp, sudden snapping sound (whip, bone, dry wood)
“The dry twig broke with a sharp crack.”






D. Human Voice and Bodily Sounds
Humans make a variety of involuntary and voluntary sounds that are captured through onomatopoeia.








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Gasp
Sudden intake of air from surprise or fear
“She gave a sharp gasp when she saw the beautiful ring.”


Giggle / Snicker
Light, silly, or suppressed laughter
“The children giggled at the clown’s silly tricks.”


Hiccup
Involuntary spasm of the diaphragm
“He drank his soda too fast and began to hiccup.”


Murmur
Low, indistinct, continuous sound
“The quiet murmur of the crowd filled the lecture hall.”


Whisper
Speaking very quietly using breath
“They had to whisper so they wouldn’t wake the sleeping baby.”


Snort
Forcing air violently through the nose (often during laughter)
“She tried to suppress her laughter but let out a loud snort.”


Sneeze / Achoo
Exploding air due to nasal irritation
“The dust made him sneeze three times in a row.”


Cough
Clearing the throat or lungs
“He gave a dry cough to clear his throat before speaking.”


Mumble
Speaking unclearly or quietly
“Stop mumbling and speak up so we can hear you.”


Sigh
Exhaling deeply to express disappointment, fatigue, or relief
“She let out a long sigh after a long day of work.”


Chuckle
Quiet, inward laugh
“The old man chuckled as he read the comic strip.”


Groan
Deep, long sound of pain, grief, or annoyance
“The audience let out a collective groan at the terrible pun.”


Burp
Releasing gas from the stomach through the mouth
“In some cultures, burping after a meal is a sign of appreciation.”


Yawn
Opening the mouth wide and inhaling due to tiredness
“He couldn’t help but yawn during the boring presentation.”






E. Motion and Air Sounds
These words describe things moving quickly through space or air passing through restricted areas.








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Whoosh
Something moving past at high speed
“The bullet train passed by the station with a loud whoosh.”


Zoom
Fast, motorized movement
“Sports cars zoomed around the racetrack.”


Whiz
Small object moving rapidly through the air
“An arrow whizzed past his ear and struck the tree.”


Flutter
Rapid, light flapping (wings, flags)
“The butterfly’s wings fluttered gently in the breeze.”


Swoosh
Smooth, sweeping sound (basketball net, swing)
“The basketball went straight through the hoop with a perfect swoosh.”


Rustle
Paper, dry leaves, or silk rubbing together
“We heard a animal rustling in the dry bushes.”


Puff
A short, explosive release of air or smoke
“The train engine let out a puff of steam as it started to move.”


Swish
Soft sweeping sound through the air
“The cat swished its tail back and forth in annoyance.”


Wheeze
Breathing with a whistling sound due to obstructed airways
“The asthmatic runner began to wheeze on the steep incline.”






F. Machine and Object Sounds
Human-made objects and mechanical processes generate distinct patterns of sound.








Word
Sound Description
Context/Example Sentence




Tick-tock
Rhythmic ticking of a clock
“The grandfather clock’s tick-tock was the only sound in the room.”


Clink
Small glass or ceramic objects touching
“They toasted their glasses with a gentle clink.”


Ding-dong
Sound of a doorbell or church bell
“The doorbell went ding-dong, announcing the guests’ arrival.”


Beep
Short, high-pitched electronic tone
“The microwave let out a sharp beep to signal the food was ready.”


Honk
Car horn or goose sound
“Frustrated drivers began to honk their horns in the traffic jam.”


Creak
Wooden floorboards or door hinges rubbing
“The old wooden stairs creaked under his weight.”


Ring
Telephone or metal bell vibrating
“I ran inside when I heard the phone ring.”


Click
Pressing a mouse, snapping a latch, or pen button
“You will hear a click when the seatbelt is locked in place.”


Whir
Rapidly spinning motor or fan
“The steady whir of the server fan filled the computer lab.”


Hum
Continuous, low vibration of machinery
“The refrigerator hums quietly in the corner.”


Screech
High-pitched sound of tires sliding or friction
“The car came to a halt with a loud screech of brakes.”


Rattle
Loose parts shaking against each other
“An old window pane rattled in the wind.”

title: Sound in Words: The Ultimate Guide to Onomatopoeia
text:
2. Grammatical Roles of Onomatopoeia
Onomatopoetic words are highly versatile. They do not just occupy a single part of speech; depending on how you structure your sentence, they can function in four main grammatical roles.

A. As Nouns
When functioning as a noun, the sound word represents the sound itself. It is often preceded by articles (a, an, the) or adjectives. * “I heard a loud bang in the basement.” * “The continuous drip of the tap was driving me crazy.” * “We listened to the gentle gurgle of the brook.”


B. As Verbs
Onomatopoetic verbs represent the action of making the sound. These verbs can be conjugated into past, present, or future tenses like any regular verb. * “The bees buzzed around the garden.” * “He slammed the door out of anger.” * “Water sloshed around in the washing machine.”


C. As Interjections
In narrative writing, comic books, or informal speech, onomatopoetic words can stand alone to punctuate an action. They are usually followed by an exclamation mark. * “Splat! The tomato hit the kitchen floor.” * “Crash! The vase shattered into a thousand pieces.” * “Achoo! Excuse me, I must be allergic to this dust.”


D. As Adjectives
By adding suffixes like -ing or using them as noun modifiers, sound words can describe nouns. * “We sat near the bubbling spring.” * “She opened a bottle of fizzing lemonade.” * “I cannot stand the creaky floorboards in this old house.”
